title_zh: 越学越棒（Learn More Gooder）｜代班主持 Mary Childs（前 NPR Planet Money）
subtitle_zh: Matt Levine 与代班主持 Mary Childs 聊 AI 如何改变房贷再融资、律所计费与 ETF 股息套利。

turns.en: Bloomberg Audio Studios. Podcasts. Radio. News.
turns.zh: Bloomberg Audio Studios。播客。广播。新闻。

turns.en: I never know how we should do the intros.
turns.zh: 我一直不知道我们该怎么开场介绍。

turns.en: Should I just, like, crawl up to the.
turns.zh: 我要不要就直接，呃，爬到那个……

turns.en: Like, you know the Monty Python hits guy? No. In Monty Python's Flying Circus, many of the episodes begin with, like, this very long, faraway shot of a, like, a haggard, like, shipwrecked man. And he gets up to the camera, like, huffing and puffing, looking like he's about to die. And he says, it's. And then it cuts to the credits.
turns.zh: 就是，你知道 Monty Python 里那个吗？不知道。在 Monty Python's Flying Circus 里，很多集都是以一个特别长、特别远的镜头开场，拍一个，呃，形容枯槁、像遭遇了海难的人。他一路连滚带爬地挪到镜头前，累得上气不接下气，一副快死了的样子。然后他说，it's（就是……）。紧接着画面就切到片头字幕了。

turns.en: That's really good.
turns.zh: 这个真不错。

turns.en: Anyway.
turns.zh: 总之。

turns.en: That's me.
turns.zh: 那说的就是我。

turns.en: That's you. I never know how to do intros because, like, we always do cold opens with Katie. But, like, it's weird to be, like, just.
turns.zh: 说的就是你。我一直不知道怎么开场，因为，呃，我们平时都是跟 Katie 一起做冷开场（cold open）。可是，呃，就这么……感觉怪怪的。

turns.en: Chatting for a while.
turns.zh: 先闲聊一阵。

turns.en: Stranger lady voice. And then be like, hello and welcome.
turns.zh: 冒出一个陌生的女声，然后说，大家好，欢迎收听。

turns.en: Surprise, that wasn't Katie.
turns.zh: 惊喜吧，那不是 Katie。

turns.en: I know, right? So. Hello and welcome to the Money Stuff podcast.
turns.zh: 就是说啊？所以。大家好，欢迎收听 Money Stuff 播客。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: I'm Matt Levine. I wrote the money stuff column for Bloomberg Opinion, and I'm joined here by my friend, Mary Childs.
turns.zh: 我是 Matt Levine。我为 Bloomberg Opinion 写 Money Stuff 专栏，今天跟我一起的是我的朋友，Mary Childs。

turns.en: Hey. Hi.
turns.zh: 嘿，你好。

turns.en: Do you want to, like, say your spiel? Do you want to, like.
turns.zh: 你要不要，呃，来一段你的开场白？你要不要，呃……

turns.en: Introduce myself, maybe?
turns.zh: 自我介绍一下，也许？

turns.en: Yeah, introduce yourself.
turns.zh: 对，自我介绍一下。

turns.en: Hi, I'm Mary Childs. I was a Bloomberg-er for six years.
turns.zh: 大家好，我是 Mary Childs。我在 Bloomberg 待过六年。

turns.en: That's where we met.
turns.zh: 我们就是在那儿认识的。

turns.en: That's where we met.
turns.zh: 我们就是在那儿认识的。

turns.en: And I was until somewhat recently a host of Planet Money, NPR's twice-weekly economics podcast. I'm a little out of breath because I was late coming here.
turns.zh: 而且直到不久前，我还是 Planet Money 的主持人，那是 NPR 每周一更两期的经济类播客。我有点上气不接下气，因为我赶来这儿迟到了。

turns.en: I sprinted. And I currently have a new show called Marian America, which is a weekly video first interview podcast, which is just a talk show.
turns.zh: 我是跑过来的。我现在有一档新节目叫 Marian America，是一档每周更新、以视频为先的访谈播客，说白了就是个脱口秀（talk show）。

turns.en: But on YouTube. But on YouTube.
turns.zh: 但是在 YouTube 上。但是在 YouTube 上。

turns.en: And we can't say talk show.
turns.zh: 而且我们不能说脱口秀。

turns.en: It's too short.
turns.zh: 太短了。

turns.en: And we talk about business, economics, finance, and also culture.
turns.zh: 我们聊商业、经济、金融，也聊文化。

turns.en: Yes, it's very good.
turns.zh: 对，这节目很好。

turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.en: So I tell people the story of how we met, which is, I think, money stuff relevant. Mm-hmm. Which is, I believe, this may not be how we literally met, but, like, I started working at Bloomberg Opinion, and I was working not in this office. Mm-hmm. And I was reading about, I'm pretty sure, Codere. I think this was Codere.
turns.zh: 所以我跟人讲我们是怎么认识的，我觉得这故事跟 Money Stuff 还挺搭。嗯哼。是这样的，我记得——这可能不是我们字面意义上认识的过程，但是，呃，我刚开始在 Bloomberg Opinion 工作，那时候我不在这个办公室。嗯哼。我当时在读一篇报道，我基本确定是关于 Codere 的。我记得就是 Codere。

turns.en: A Spanish gambling company.
turns.zh: 一家西班牙的博彩公司。

turns.en: A Spanish gambling company that did some wild stuff to manipulate at CDS.
turns.zh: 一家西班牙博彩公司，为了操纵 CDS（信用违约互换，credit default swap）干了些很离谱的事。

turns.en: Very fun times.
turns.zh: 那段日子很有意思。

turns.en: And, like, some hedge fund person, someone told me something about it, and I was like, that's amazing. Mm-hmm. And I was like, who can I tell this? And so I called you up and I was like, can I just gossip with you about a credit default swap trade? And you're like, is it Codere? So you and I have been friends for a long time. It's true. And you have been a professional podcaster for some of that time. That's true. Also true. And during that time. You have never had me on a podcast, although now I have you on my podcast.
turns.zh: 然后，呃，某个对冲基金的人，有人跟我说了这事儿，我就觉得，太神了。嗯哼。我就想，我能跟谁聊这个？于是我就给你打电话，我说，我能不能就跟你八卦一下这笔信用违约互换的交易？你就说，是 Codere 那事儿吗？所以我们俩当朋友已经很久了。真的。而且这段时间里，你有一阵子是职业播客主持人。没错。也是真的。而且在那期间，你从来没请我上过你的播客，尽管现在我请你上了我的播客。

turns.en: I had a policy.
turns.zh: 我是有个原则的。

turns.en: I had a save Matt Levine for emergencies policy, but I guess I never had an emergency yet.
turns.zh: 我的原则是把 Matt Levine 留着应急，但看样子我一直还没碰上什么紧急情况。

turns.en: Alas. Alas. Yeah. Anyway, what are you going to talk about?
turns.zh: 唉。唉。是啊。总之，你打算聊点什么？

turns.en: Well, you have the paper.
turns.zh: 呃，你手上有那篇论文。

turns.en: I don't know. A lot of AI stuff. But one is, there was a great Bloomberg story last week about the effect of AI on mortgage refinancing.
turns.zh: 我也不知道。有很多 AI 相关的东西。不过其中一个是，上周 Bloomberg 有篇很棒的报道，讲 AI 对住房抵押贷款再融资（mortgage refinancing）的影响。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: It's based on this Morgan Stanley research. But so the idea is, broadly speaking, people do not refinance their mortgages optimally.
turns.zh: 这篇报道是基于 Morgan Stanley 的一项研究。大致意思是，总的来说，人们并不会最优地去给自己的房贷做再融资。

turns.en: They really don't. And it's a point of frustration for me personally.
turns.zh: 他们真的不会。而且这件事让我个人挺抓狂的。

turns.en: Why?
turns.zh: 为什么？

turns.en: I was on a plane the other day and this man was telling me for some reason, I don't know what I did to him, but he was telling me his mortgage rate and that he needs to buy a bigger house.
turns.zh: 前几天我在飞机上，有个男的不知怎么就——我也不知道我做了什么让他这样——他一直跟我讲他的房贷利率，还说他需要买套更大的房子。

turns.en: And I was like, what is it? And he was like, it's like two point. And I was like, do not sell that house. He can't sell it. He's going to do it. He wouldn't listen to me. I feel like I'm going one by one and meeting people with low interest rate mortgages, rates that are lower than where rates are today. So if they buy a new house, they're going to get a higher rate. Sorry, I forgot what audience this is. I don't need to say that.
turns.zh: 我就问，是多少啊？他说，大概两点几（two point）。我就说，千万别卖那套房子。可他没法不卖。他就是要卖。他根本不听我的。我感觉我像是在一个一个地碰到那些背着低利率房贷的人，利率比现在的水平还低。所以如果他们买新房，就会拿到更高的利率。抱歉，我忘了这是讲给什么听众听的。这些话我不必说。

turns.en: Okay, so that's true. But that I sympathize with because sometimes you need a different house.
turns.zh: 好吧，这是真的。不过这一点我很能理解，因为有时候你就是需要换一套房子。

turns.en: No, build onto your house.
turns.zh: 不，你该在原来那套上加盖。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好吧。

turns.en: Sorry. I'm sorry. It's a strongly held belief. I can't do anything about it.
turns.zh: 抱歉。真抱歉。这是我根深蒂固的信念，我也没办法。

turns.en: Like I said, I sympathize with people who leave their houses with low mortgage rates and go to houses with higher mortgage rates because they need a bigger house or a house in a different place.
turns.zh: 就像我说的，我很理解那些人，他们离开自己那套低利率房贷的房子，换成利率更高的房子，是因为他们需要一套更大的房子，或者换个地方的房子。

turns.en: Are you saying that you did this?
turns.zh: 你是在说你自己就这么干了？

turns.en: No. Yeah, you didn't do this. I keep looking at real estate.
turns.zh: 没有。对，你没这么干。我一直在看房产。

turns.en: Oh, you're trying to do this.
turns.zh: 哦，你是正打算这么干。

turns.en: Even though I have like a sub 3% mortgage.
turns.zh: 尽管我的房贷利率还不到 3%。

turns.en: That's handcuffs, right?
turns.zh: 那就是副手铐，对吧？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Golden handcuffs or whatever.
turns.zh: 金手铐（golden handcuffs）之类的。

turns.en: But the thing that people do really suboptimally is when rates go down.
turns.zh: 但人们真正做得很不最优的，是利率下降的时候。

turns.en: Right. They don't do anything.
turns.zh: 对。他们什么都不做。

turns.en: They don't do anything.
turns.zh: 他们什么都不做。

turns.en: And they should.
turns.zh: 而他们本该做点什么。

turns.en: And they should. And the Morgan Stanley thesis is that rates right now are like, let's say high-ish.
turns.zh: 他们本该做。而 Morgan Stanley 的论点是，现在的利率，就比如说，算是偏高。

turns.en: I feel like they're very high.
turns.zh: 我觉得是非常高。

turns.en: They're high compared to like recent history. I'm not sure they're high in like the grand scheme of things. That's true. But so they're like, if rates go down again- mortgage refinancing is going to be a lot easier than it was last time with rates went down because like all these like mortgage companies have invested in like ai tools to make the process easier so it's like 10 minutes to refinance your morgans instead of like two weeks and also i think like one clear reason that people don't refinance their mortgages is just inattention right like people don't pay attention to mortgages they don't understand like the.
turns.zh: 跟近几年的历史比是高。我不确定放到更长的大势里算不算高。这倒是。但所以说，如果利率再往下走——房贷再融资会比上一次利率下降时容易得多，因为所有这些房贷公司都投资了 AI 工具来让流程更简单，所以再融资只要 10 分钟，而不是像过去要两周。而且我觉得，人们不去做房贷再融资，一个很明确的原因就是没上心（inattention），对吧，人们根本不注意房贷这回事，他们也不理解那个……

turns.en: They're not sitting next to me on a plane yeah and they should.
turns.zh: 他们又没在飞机上坐我旁边，是啊，其实他们就该被人这么念叨一下。

turns.en: And it's possible that like sort of like waving my hands and Literally like, like vaguing over this, but like possibly like in a world with more AI, like somehow your AI agents will be like, Hey buddy, time to refinance your mortgage. Now rates have fallen by 200 basis points or whatever. And so there's some notion that like right now people really, really, really do not optimally refinance their mortgages. And in some sort of AI world, they will be much more likely to. And so one, that's kind of interesting too. It's very bad for mortgage investors because right now, like, there's this refinance option in every mortgage, right, where, like, you have the option to refinance basically without penalty. And people exercise it really suboptimally. And so it is not priced. Like, if you, like, just did an interest rate model, you would charge people a lot for that option and, like, the interest rate of the mortgage. But, like, you don't because they don't exercise it optimally. And if they did, then mortgages would be more expensive. Morgan Stanley says 10 to 20 basis points more expensive for everybody.
turns.zh: 而且有可能——这我算是挥挥手、含糊带过了——但有可能在一个 AI 更多的世界里，不知怎么你的 AI 智能体（AI agent）就会说，'嘿，伙计，该给房贷再融资了。现在利率已经降了 200 个基点（basis points）'之类的。所以有一种说法是，眼下人们真的、真的、真的不会最优地做房贷再融资。而在某种 AI 世界里，他们会更有可能去做。所以，一是，这本身就挺有意思。二是对房贷投资者非常不利，因为现在每笔房贷里都嵌着一个再融资期权（refinance option），对吧，你有权基本无罚金地再融资。而人们行使得非常不最优。所以这个期权没有被定价进去。就是说，如果你只做一个利率模型，你会为这个期权向人们收很多钱，加到房贷利率里。但你没那么做，因为他们行使得不最优。而如果他们最优行使了，房贷就会更贵。Morgan Stanley 说，对每个人来说会贵 10 到 20 个基点。

turns.en: And this builds on research by Fabrice Touré, formerly of Goldman Sachs, now at, I forgot what university.
turns.zh: 而这建立在 Fabrice Touré 的研究基础上，他以前在 Goldman Sachs，现在在——我忘了是哪所大学了。

turns.en: I think he's at Baruch. Anyway, Fabulous Fab, who is now a finance academic, but was previously a mortgage derivative structure at Goldman Sachs, where he got in some trouble for structuring some mortgage derivatives.
turns.zh: 我记得他在 Baruch。总之，Fabulous Fab（'了不起的 Fab'），他现在是个金融学学者，但之前在 Goldman Sachs 做房贷衍生品结构化（mortgage derivative structurer），还因为设计了一些房贷衍生品而惹上了麻烦。

turns.en: Well, who better to know when retail investors are not making sense?
turns.zh: 那还有谁比他更清楚散户投资者（retail investors）什么时候在犯傻呢？

turns.en: Who better to know? And he wrote this paper about, he's the co-author of the paper, Refinancing Frictions, Mortgage Pricing, and Redistribution. And one thing that the abstract of the paper says is, many policies that lead to more frequent refinancing also increase equilibrium mortgage rates and thus reduce residential mortgage credit access for a large number of borrowers. That is, if you make it easier for people to refinance their mortgages, then... Mortgage rates will go up because they will refinance more optimally and mortgages will be more expensive, more negative convexity. And so investors will like them less. And so they will charge more for them. Yeah.
turns.zh: 还有谁更清楚？他写了这篇论文，他是这篇论文的共同作者，题目是《Refinancing Frictions, Mortgage Pricing, and Redistribution》（再融资摩擦、房贷定价与再分配）。论文摘要里有一点说，许多促使再融资更频繁的政策，也会推高均衡房贷利率，从而减少大量借款人获得住房抵押贷款信贷的机会。也就是说，如果你让人们更容易给房贷再融资，那么……房贷利率就会上升，因为他们会更好地行使再融资，房贷就会更贵，负凸性（negative convexity）更多。于是投资者就更不喜欢它们。于是就会为它们收更高的价。对。

turns.en: So it's like bad for society for people to be if you believe in it.
turns.zh: 所以，如果你信这套的话，让人们（最优行使）对社会反而是不好的。

turns.en: Oh, your face. If you think when your face goes dead a little bit.
turns.zh: 哦，你的表情。你想这事的时候，脸都有点僵了。

turns.en: It either means you really don't. If you want a society where people own their homes, which has historically been a great vehicle for wealth creation in this country. then you want mortgage rates to be subsidized in this way. And if you have people who optimally exercise their options and the market has to reprice based on that, fewer people are going to have access to mortgages and houses.
turns.zh: 这要么说明你是真不信。如果你想要一个人人都拥有自己住房的社会——拥有住房在这个国家历来是很棒的财富创造途径——那你就希望房贷利率以这种方式被补贴。而如果人们最优地行使他们的期权，市场又不得不据此重新定价，那么能拿到房贷、买得起房子的人就会更少。

turns.en: Yeah. And like this has come up a lot in recent years the other way, right? So like Morgan Stanley is really talking about when rates drop, people optimally refinancing. But like right now, rates have gone up in the last few years and people have been really... Boxed out. Yeah. And then people have been like really antsy about that and have thought about ways to unbox them out. So like if you have like assumable mortgages where like if I have a 3% mortgage and I sell you my house, you can keep my mortgage, right?
turns.zh: 对。而且这几年这个话题也以另一种方式反复出现，对吧。所以 Morgan Stanley 说的其实是利率下降时人们最优地再融资。但现在，过去几年利率是往上涨的，人们一直被……卡住（boxed out）。对。然后大家就特别着急，想方设法把他们从这个困局里解出来。所以比如说，如果有可承接的房贷（assumable mortgages），就是如果我有一笔 3% 的房贷，我把房子卖给你，你可以保留我这笔房贷，对吧？

turns.en: I love that.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个了。

turns.en: You love that, but that would make mortgages more expensive in the future, right? Because it's the same thing. It's like you would have more optimal exercise and therefore the option would be more valuable and therefore mortgages would be more expensive.
turns.zh: 你喜欢这个，但那会让未来的房贷更贵，对吧？因为是一回事。就是说，你会有更最优的行使，因此这个期权就更有价值，因此房贷就会更贵。

turns.en: In Switzerland, you can take your mortgage with you.
turns.zh: 在瑞士，你可以把房贷随身带走。

turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.en: I wanted to do a Planet Money survey of the whole world of like, what's the best, most fun, crazy thing your mortgage market does?
turns.zh: 我一直想在 Planet Money 做个全球调查，就是问，你们房贷市场里最棒、最好玩、最疯狂的做法是什么？

turns.en: But I didn't do it. It's a lot of work.
turns.zh: 但我没做。工作量太大了。

turns.en: Right. The best, most crazy thing the U.S. mortgage market does is offer 30-year fixed rate mortgages that are prepayable.
turns.zh: 对。美国房贷市场最棒、最疯狂的做法，就是提供可提前偿还（prepayable）的 30 年期固定利率房贷。

turns.en: It's like a very.
turns.zh: 这就像一个非常……

turns.en: Very, very subsidized product. And one way it's subsidized is just like institutional structures, but one way it's subsidized is by the fact that people do not exercise it optimally. Reading this thing, I loved it in part because that prepay option is really big and interesting, but also because so much of consumer finance is like this. Credit card rewards are like this.
turns.zh: 非常、非常被补贴的产品。它被补贴的一种方式就是制度结构，但另一种补贴方式就是人们并没有最优地行使它。读这篇东西的时候我特别喜欢它，一部分是因为那个提前偿还期权（prepay option）真的很大、很有意思，但也是因为消费金融里有太多东西都是这样的。信用卡奖励（credit card rewards）就是这样。

turns.en: I know.
turns.zh: 我知道。

turns.en: Reading it, you cited the Capital One example of a relatively high APR.
turns.zh: 读的时候，你引用了 Capital One 那个 APR（年化利率）相对偏高的例子。

turns.en: I'm a Capital One customer. I think I'm there.
turns.zh: 我就是 Capital One 的客户。我觉得说的就是我。

turns.en: I think that I'm the person being written about not optimally exercising my, I should be shopping for a higher rate.
turns.zh: 我觉得我就是那个被写进去的人——没有最优地行使我的（期权），我本该去货比三家找个更高的利率。

turns.en: It's easy to be like, oh, people are not paying attention or being stupid. But in your actual life, there's a lot of rational ignorance, right? I knew a guy at Goldman who like, Every week would check the highest yielding high-yield savings accounts.
turns.zh: 你很容易就说，哦，人们是没上心或者犯傻。但在你真实的生活中，有大量理性的无知（rational ignorance），对吧？我在 Goldman 认识一个人，他，呃，每周都会去查收益率最高的高收益储蓄账户（high-yield savings accounts）。

turns.en: I love that about him.
turns.zh: 我就喜欢他这一点。

turns.en: And would move his money from the one paying like 5% to the one paying like 5.05%. But most people don't do that.
turns.zh: 然后他会把钱从付 5% 左右的那家挪到付 5.05% 左右的那家。但大多数人不会这么做。

turns.en: Was he fun or not fun?
turns.zh: 他这人有趣还是不有趣？

turns.en: Very fun. Okay, see? I mean, not in a traditional sense.
turns.zh: 非常有趣。看吧？我是说，不是传统意义上的那种有趣。

turns.en: Was it Goose?
turns.zh: 是 Goose 吗？

turns.en: I liked him. Just kidding. No, it wasn't Goose.
turns.zh: 我挺喜欢他的。开玩笑的。不，不是 Goose。

turns.en: Hi, Goose.
turns.zh: 嗨，Goose。

turns.en: I'm keeping that all in. But, you know, I don't check my rates every week. But maybe we should. I don't have to, like, change my password.
turns.zh: 这些我都会保留在正片里。不过，你知道，我不会每周去查我的利率。但也许我们该查查。我又不必，呃，改我的密码。

turns.en: Maybe you should have an AI agent that scrapes for you.
turns.zh: 也许你该弄个 AI 智能体帮你抓取比价。

turns.en: Well, this is the thing. Like, this is the thing that the Morgan Stanley Note is making me think of is, like, in the future, all this stuff gets more frictionless. And, like, I read a lot about, like, retail brokerage stuff where, like, agentic trading will make trading much more frictionless and therefore … you will lose just bushels of money because you'll be trading all the time, right? But I think in other ways, making it easy to move to the highest yielding, high yield savings account will.
turns.zh: 嗯，这就是关键。这就是 Morgan Stanley 那份报告让我想到的：未来，所有这些事情都会变得更无摩擦（frictionless）。我读了很多关于零售券商（retail brokerage）的东西，就是那种智能体交易（agentic trading）会让交易变得无摩擦得多，因此……你会亏掉一大堆钱，因为你会一直在交易，对吧？但我觉得在别的方面，让你更容易转到收益率最高的高收益储蓄账户，这会……

turns.en: I want that.
turns.zh: 我想要这个。

turns.en: It'll make you some money, but it'll also like... Save you brain space. Yeah, but it'll also like break the way the financial system works because... like the system right now is set up around a certain level of like non-optimal exercise of all these options. And like if everyone has AI agents to exercise everything optimally, then like it'll get weird.
turns.zh: 它会帮你赚点钱，但它也会……帮你省下脑力（brain space）。对，但它也会……打破金融系统现在的运作方式，因为……现在的系统是围绕着某种程度的、对所有这些期权的不最优行使而搭建起来的。而如果人人都有 AI 智能体去最优地行使一切，那么……事情就会变得很奇怪。

turns.en: What do you think they're doing about this? They've got to know, right?
turns.zh: 你觉得他们对此在做什么应对？他们肯定知道，对吧？

turns.en: Well, there's no they.
turns.zh: 嗯，其实并不存在一个'他们'。

turns.en: I know, but there's a lot of they.
turns.zh: 我知道，但'他们'可不少。

turns.en: Like one thing they are doing about this is Morgan Stanley writing this note Which says things like historical prepay behavior will understate future prepays. So models trained on the past mispriced this option that borrowers will be more inclined to exercise. So one thing they're saying is like don't buy mortgages at like current model prices because like you'll have to reprice everything for like higher exercise rates. But it's going to be the same in like insurance and savings accounts.
turns.zh: 比如说，他们对此在做的一件事，就是 Morgan Stanley 写了这份报告，里面说，历史上的提前偿还行为会低估未来的提前偿还。所以基于过去训练的模型错误定价了这个期权，借款人会更倾向于行使它。所以他们说的其中一点是，别按当前的模型价格买房贷，因为你得把一切都重新定价，以反映更高的行使率。但保险和储蓄账户也会是一样。

turns.en: Not to bring this back to PIMCO.
turns.zh: 不是要把话题拉回 PIMCO 啊。

turns.en: That's the first mention of PIMCO. Mary wrote a book about PIMCO. I did.
turns.zh: 这是第一次提到 PIMCO。Mary 写过一本关于 PIMCO 的书。我写过。

turns.en: I did.
turns.zh: 我写过。

turns.en: And I've worked really hard to think about other things in the intervening years. But Scott Simon was a mortgage trader at PIMCO, one of the very admired mortgage traders of that cohort, that generation, pre- and post-crisis. And he had a little suitcase that had his own little computer in it with his model, with his mortgage-backed security investing model in it.
turns.zh: 而且这些年我一直很努力地让自己去想别的事情。但 Scott Simon 曾是 PIMCO 的房贷交易员，是那一代、那一批人里非常受推崇的房贷交易员之一，危机前后都是。他有个小手提箱，里面装着他自己的小电脑，电脑里是他的模型，他的抵押贷款支持证券（mortgage-backed security）投资模型。

turns.en: Cool.
turns.zh: 酷。

turns.en: And I know, and he would not plug it in. That's how valued these models are. His little special model, which is the whole basis of why he was good, he wouldn't even plug it in at his own employer. That's so good. That's all for PIMCO for today.
turns.zh: 而且我知道，他压根不会把它插上电。这些模型就是这么金贵。他那个小小的、特别的模型，是他厉害的全部根基，他甚至不肯在自己东家那儿把它插上电。这太绝了。今天关于 PIMCO 就聊到这儿。

turns.en: We'll see, we'll see. But yeah, so what are they going to do? I don't know. What are they going to do? I don't think there will be a they making a decision all at once.
turns.zh: 走着瞧吧，走着瞧。不过是啊，那他们打算怎么办？我不知道。他们打算怎么办？我不觉得会有一个'他们'一次性做出决定。

turns.en: No, there's a person at Capital One who's like, shh.
turns.zh: 不，Capital One 那儿是有个人在说，嘘。

turns.en: Yeah, I think options are going to be repriced. I think mortgages... Like if it actually becomes easier to prepay mortgages, like mortgages will get more expensive. I think if it actually becomes easier to– I love the phrase optimally exercise life insurance because it's very– but if it becomes easier to optimally exercise life insurance, which means basically not let it lapse when it's positive expected value, then life insurance will get more expensive.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得期权会被重新定价。我觉得房贷……如果提前偿还房贷真的变得更容易，房贷就会更贵。我觉得如果……我特别喜欢'最优地行使人寿保险'这个说法，因为它非常——但如果最优地行使人寿保险变得更容易，也就是基本上在预期价值为正的时候不让保单失效（lapse），那么人寿保险就会更贵。

turns.en: It means figure out a way to die without dying, which AI could probably help with.
turns.zh: 那就是说想办法在不真死的情况下'死'一次，这事儿 AI 说不定能帮上忙。

turns.en: No, it means like the suboptimal exercise of life insurance is you buy term life insurance and then you stop paying the premiums and then you die later.
turns.zh: 不，它的意思是，人寿保险的不最优行使，就是你买了定期寿险（term life insurance），然后你停止交保费，再然后你后来去世了。

turns.en: Right, right. Or you pay all the premiums and you die after the term.
turns.zh: 对，对。或者你交完了所有保费，却在保险期结束后才去世。

turns.en: But that's not a flaw in your exercise of the option.
turns.zh: 但那并不是你行使期权时的一个缺陷。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: You didn't exercise it. Yeah.
turns.zh: 你根本没行使它。对。

turns.en: If you buy a 20-year term life.
turns.zh: 如果你买一份 20 年期的定期寿险。

turns.en: And die at 21.
turns.zh: 然后在第 21 年去世。

turns.en: Truly, if you buy a 20-year term life and you die at 21 years, that's fine. Like, that's how it's supposed to be. Oh, really? Yeah. Because you're providing for your kids. Oh, I see.
turns.zh: 说真的，如果你买一份 20 年期定期寿险，然后在第 21 年去世，那没问题。本来就该是这样。真的吗？对。因为你是在为你的孩子提供保障。哦，我明白了。

turns.en: It's just you enjoyed the— okay.
turns.zh: 只是你享受了那个——好吧。

turns.en: There's a reason people buy term life rather than universal life, and it's because there is a window where it would be very economically bad for their beneficiaries.
turns.zh: 人们买定期寿险（term life）而不是万能寿险（universal life）是有原因的，那是因为存在一个时间窗口，在那个窗口里（若去世）对受益人（beneficiaries）来说经济上会非常糟糕。

turns.en: Beneficiaries.
turns.zh: 受益人。

turns.en: But then after that window, it's fine. Dish, you know, economically. Okay. Can I talk about AI and law firms? Yes. This is a great Financial Times story this week about... It's so rude. All the big banks are like... Excuse me. This is like a general thing is like every company is putting pressure on all of its service providers. It's like professional services firms to cut prices because they can use AI. And so if you hire consultants or you hire investment bankers, you're like, you don't need an army of people to do this stuff. You have AI do it. So charges lower rates. Right. But with law firms, I think it's really interesting because Law firms bill by the hour. Right.
turns.zh: 但过了那个窗口，就没问题了。你懂的，经济上没问题。好。我能聊聊 AI 和律所吗？能。这周《Financial Times》有篇很棒的报道，讲的是……太没礼貌了。所有大银行都在……不好意思。这是件很普遍的事，就是每家公司都在给它所有的服务商施压。就是那些专业服务公司（professional services firms），逼他们降价，因为他们可以用 AI。所以如果你雇咨询顾问或者雇投资银行家，你就会说，你不需要一大帮人来干这些活儿。你让 AI 干。所以要收更低的费率。对。但说到律所，我觉得特别有意思，因为律所是按小时计费（bill by the hour）的。对。

turns.en: And— AI saves you time.
turns.zh: 而——AI 帮你省时间。

turns.en: And AI saves you time. But, like, I think it's particularly interesting, and I wrote about this, is, like, law firms kind of fake bill by the hour. Like, they bill by the hour. But, like, the way a, like, law firm partner makes money is not by billing out her time, but it's by, like, having an army of associates who work for her and billing out their time, right? Mm-hmm. And then paying them less than them. Yeah, and paying them less than their hourly rate. Well, she gets more than her hourly rate. And, like, what's happening there is not, like, companies are like, ooh, I want to hire associates and the only way I can hire associates is through this law firm partner. Like, that's not what's happening. What's happening is the companies are hiring the law firm partner and they really value her advice or, like, litigation skills or whatever.
turns.zh: 而 AI 帮你省时间。但，呃，我觉得特别有意思的是——我也写过这个——律所其实是有点假装按小时计费的。就是说，他们按小时计费。但，呃，一个律所合伙人（law firm partner）赚钱的方式，不是靠把自己的时间计费出去，而是靠手下有一大批替她干活的初级律师（associates），把他们的时间计费出去，对吧？嗯哼。然后付给他们的钱比（客户付的）少。对，付给他们的比他们的小时费率低。呃，而她拿到的比她的小时费率还高。这里发生的并不是，公司说，哦，我想雇一批 associates，而我唯一能雇到 associates 的途径就是通过这个律所合伙人。不是那样的。真正发生的是，公司雇的是这位律所合伙人，他们非常看重她的建议，或者她的诉讼技巧之类的。

turns.en: Expertise.
turns.zh: 专业知识。

turns.en: But, like, to get her, they need to pay a lot of hours of her associates, like, doing grunt work. And if all the grunt work can be done by AI, then, like, that model doesn't work. And that doesn't mean... That like the law firm partner can't still charge them a lot of money for her expertise and trial skills or whatever. It just means you have to, it can't be by the hour anymore. It can't be by the associate hour anymore. You got to like change the billing model.
turns.zh: 但，呃，为了得到她，他们就得为她手下一大批做苦力活儿（grunt work）的 associates 付很多小时的钱。而如果所有苦力活儿都能由 AI 来干，那么……这个模式就行不通了。这并不意味着……那位律所合伙人就不能再靠她的专业知识和庭审技巧之类收一大笔钱。这只是意味着，你没法再按小时计费了。没法再按 associate 的小时计费了。你得，呃，改变计费模式。

turns.en: It also means what are they going to do in the future when they have no one who's been trained? Like when there's no junior person learning from her.
turns.zh: 这也意味着，将来当他们没有任何受过训练的人时，该怎么办？就是当没有初级的人跟着她学习的时候。

turns.en: I know. So what happens next?
turns.zh: 我知道。那接下来会怎样？

turns.en: This is every professional service firm is like an apprenticeship model.
turns.zh: 这就是说，每一家专业服务公司都像一个学徒制（apprenticeship）模式。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And the good story that everyone tells is like, no, no, we'll maybe hire fewer. junior people.
turns.zh: 而大家都讲的那个美好版本是，不不，我们也许会少雇一些。初级的人。

turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.en: But we'll still hire a lot. And those people will not do as much grunt work, but they will have higher level work. They'll supervise the AI models. They'll learn more good or faster. They'll learn more good or faster. Good. And then they'll become really good partners one day themselves. That's great. Okay.
turns.zh: 但我们还是会雇很多。而且这些人不会做那么多苦力活儿，但他们会有更高层级的工作。他们会监督 AI 模型。他们会学得更好、更快，也就是 more good or faster。他们会学得 more good or faster。很好。然后有一天他们自己会成为非常出色的合伙人。那太好了。好。

turns.en: I don't need to worry.
turns.zh: 那我就不用担心了。

turns.en: And like, you can think of examples of that. Like the example I always think of is like investment bank analysts. We're like, what do investment bank analysts do that trains them to become senior investment bankers. One thing they do is like format PowerPoint presentations.
turns.zh: 而且，呃，你能想到这样的例子。我一直想到的例子就是投行分析师（investment bank analysts）。我们会说，投行分析师做的哪些事，是在训练他们成为资深投行人士。他们做的一件事，就是给 PowerPoint 演示文稿排版。

turns.en: I was about to say, make sure it's flush left.
turns.zh: 我正要说，确保它左对齐（flush left）。

turns.en: Yes. And probably if an AI does that really well, then like the junior bankers will have more time to devote to high level work.
turns.zh: 对。而且很可能，如果 AI 把这事干得非常好，那么初级银行家（junior bankers）就会有更多时间投入到高层级的工作上。

turns.en: To using their brain. That's wonderful.
turns.zh: 去用他们的脑子。那太棒了。

turns.en: And will become better senior bankers and like not getting the experience of like formatting PowerPoints.
turns.zh: 并且会成为更出色的资深银行家，而并没有那种，呃，给 PowerPoint 排版的经历。

turns.en: It's probably okay.
turns.zh: 这大概没关系。

turns.en: Is fine. Yeah. But the other thing they do is like build financial models, right? And senior investment bankers are not spending a lot of time building like three statement models and like, you know, testing sensitivities for, but, like, the experience of that is really valuable and, like, makes you more intuitive at, like, helping companies, you know, do strategic planning and, like, negotiate mergers. And, like, if you lose that, then that makes it much harder to become a good senior banker. And I think there's stuff like that everywhere, right? Like, in law firms, like, a lot of the stuff that junior associates do feels really pointless drudgery and is not, like, related to, like, developing trial strategy, but like a lot of it is, right? And like you have to put in the hundreds of hours of drudgery to become a good senior strategist or whatever. And if you cut out both of those, like it's hard to know where the apprenticeship model goes.
turns.zh: 是没关系的。对。但他们做的另一件事，是搭建财务模型（financial models），对吧？而资深投行人士并不会花很多时间去搭那种三张报表联动的模型（three statement models），也不会去，你懂的，测试敏感性。但那种经历其实非常有价值，会让你在帮助公司做战略规划、谈判并购（mergers）时更有直觉。而如果你失去了那种经历，那就更难成为一名出色的资深银行家。我觉得到处都是这样的东西，对吧？比如在律所，很多初级 associates 做的活儿感觉像是极其无聊的苦差事，跟制定庭审策略没什么关系，但其实很多是有关系的，对吧？你得熬过那几百个小时的苦差事，才能成为一个优秀的资深策略家之类的。而如果你把这两样都砍掉了，那就很难知道这个学徒制模式会走向何方。

turns.en: It's also hard to know exactly where all of the tasks fall on that spectrum between dumb and fungible and it's okay to hand it to the AI versus expertise necessary.
turns.zh: 而且也很难确切知道，所有那些任务落在这条谱系上的哪个位置——一端是又笨又可替代、交给 AI 也无所谓的，另一端是必需的专业能力。

turns.en: Also, it's like, it's not clear that like the stuff that is the most drudgery is the stuff that is most easy to hand to the AI. And the stuff that's, like, highest level and smartest is the stuff that, like, one thing you can hand to the AI is, like, write a brief, right? And they'll write a brief, right? And that's, like, the best work for the junior associates, right? And then if it's, like, review these handwritten notes that, like, our clients wrote when they were doing their crimes, like, maybe the AI has trouble reviewing the handwritten notes.
turns.zh: 而且，呃，也并不清楚，那些最像苦差事的活儿，就是最容易交给 AI 的活儿。而那些最高层级、最聪明的活儿……呃，你能交给 AI 的一件事，就是写一份法律简报（brief），对吧？它们会写一份简报，对吧？而那其实是初级 associates 最好的活儿之一，对吧？然后如果是那种，审阅我们客户当年犯罪时写下的手写笔记，那可能 AI 审阅这些手写笔记就有困难了。

turns.en: Right, or, like, converse and detect intonation. Right.
turns.zh: 对，或者，呃，交谈、察觉语气（intonation）。对。

turns.en: Uh-oh. So it's possible that, like, the drudgery stays with the associates and the good work gets handed off to the AI.
turns.zh: 哎呀。所以有可能，呃，那些苦差事还留在 associates 手里，而好的活儿反倒交给了 AI。

turns.en: Yeah. There have also been recent stories about this guy from Quinn Emanuel. He was there for over a decade. Do you know Chris Kircher? He just left Quinn Emanuel to.
turns.zh: 对。最近也有关于 Quinn Emanuel 那家伙的报道。他在那儿待了十几年。你认识 Chris Kircher 吗？他刚离开 Quinn Emanuel，去……

turns.en: Start an AI, a new shaped law firm for this exact reason.
turns.zh: 创办一家 AI 的、全新形态的律所，正是出于这个原因。

turns.en: Your face.
turns.zh: 你的表情。

turns.en: Right. No, I mean, like, right. So like one answer to the question of like, where does the apprenticeship model go? And like, how do you get new partners? If there are, you know, like, I think that what happens is that the big banks, the big law firms continue to take in junior people. and train them. Maybe they take in fewer, maybe the training is different, maybe you miss out on some aspects of it, but like they're aware of this problem. It will go on, yeah. And they're trying to generate new partners because they have a perpetual existence. But I also think that a lot of like, like it's much easier if you're like a managing director at a bank or a partner at a law firm to be like, I don't need any of this. I'm going to go off and be a boutique with like six AI agents and just meet, right? And like, If enough of the top people split off to do that, then that also kind of undermines the apprenticeship model at the big places. Right. Like if you're like a partner in a big law firm, I don't need these associates. I don't need like the partnership committee. I don't need it. I just have an AI. Maybe that makes it harder for the big firms to survive. Well, like to compete and to train their people and all this stuff. Yeah. It's all pretty speculative.
turns.zh: 对。不，我是说，对吧。所以对于'学徒制模式会走向何方'这个问题，一个答案是……以及你怎么培养出新的合伙人？如果有的话，你懂的……呃，我觉得会发生的是，大银行、大律所会继续招收初级的人，并训练他们。也许他们招得更少，也许训练方式不同，也许你会错过其中某些方面，但他们清楚这个问题。它会延续下去，对。而且他们在努力培养新的合伙人，因为他们是永续存在的（perpetual existence）。但我也觉得，很多……呃，如果你是银行里的董事总经理（managing director）或者律所的合伙人，你更容易说，我不需要这些了。我要出去单干，做一个精品店（boutique），配上大概六个 AI 智能体，就靠见面谈，对吧？而如果足够多的顶尖人才都分出去这么干，那这也会在一定程度上削弱大机构里的学徒制模式。对。就是说，如果你是大律所的合伙人，我不需要这些 associates 了。我不需要那个合伙人委员会（partnership committee）。我不需要它。我只要有个 AI 就行。也许这会让大律所更难生存。呃，更难竞争、更难培养他们的人，以及所有这些。对。这一切都相当是推测。

turns.en: Exciting, though.
turns.zh: 不过挺令人兴奋的。

But anyway, Amazon does online ads and they run auctions for spots. And basically like the FTC's contention is that they say they run a second price auction where like the highest bidder in the auction gets the ad spot, but it pays the price that was bid by the second highest bidder. And the FTC says that's actually not true. And it's like 80% of cases, the winning bidder gets the, um, quote, soft reserve.
turns.zh: 所以总之，我当时想，哦，我们（金融）是这样搞拍卖的，但其实不是，真正懂拍卖的是那些做在线广告的人。不过总之，Amazon 做在线广告，他们为广告位办拍卖。基本上，FTC 的主张是，他们说他们搞的是第二价格拍卖（second price auction），就是拍卖里出价最高的人拿到广告位，但付的是第二高出价者的价格。而 FTC 说这其实并不属实。而且在大约 80% 的情况下，中标者拿到的是那个，呃，所谓的软保留价（soft reserve）。

turns.en: It pays its own price. Yeah.
turns.zh: 它付的是它自己的价格。对。

turns.en: It doesn't pay the soft reserve. It pays its own highest bid, which is because, in fact, Amazon introduces a thing called a soft reserve price, which is sort of like a phantom bid where it's like Amazon's bid. It's what Amazon thinks the slot is worth.
turns.zh: 它付的不是软保留价。它付的是它自己的最高出价，这是因为，事实上，Amazon 引入了一个叫软保留价（soft reserve price）的东西，它有点像是一个幽灵出价（phantom bid），就是 Amazon 自己的出价。它是 Amazon 认为这个广告位值多少钱。

turns.en: If we were bidding in our own auction.
turns.zh: 就好像我们自己在自家的拍卖里出价一样。

turns.en: Right. So if you bid more than the soft reserve price, then you get the soft reserve price because that's the second best bid. And if you bid less than the soft reserve price, then you get your price because that's the second best bid. So in any case, you get the second best bid, but in an auction with an extra bidder who bids high. And so the FTC finds this decisive. And I think Amazon's defense is fascinating because they don't say like, we don't do that. They do say, we disclose it clearly. You know, they say, we actually are not lying about this. Like we actually disclose things. But you know, the FTC quotes all these things where they like send out like educational materials explaining second price auctions to advertisers. And the FTC is like, but that's not what you do. And Amazon's like, look, Nobody buys ads based on like simplified descriptions of the auction mechanics. They buy ads based on like return on ad spend, right? So if you spend a dollar and you get $ 4 of revenue, you're like, yeah, great. I'll keep buying ads. Amazon's defense here, which I think is true. And it's just interesting to me because it's like not how the financial industry works. Amazon's defense is like, basically this is a black box. We do not expect our advertisers to actually understand like the auction mechanics because like what we're doing is not a second price auction, right? It's like, sure, it's a second-price auction with a soft reserve price, but we don't even know the soft reserve price until after. It's computed in real time. So no one can know if they're going to be the second-best price or the first-best price. But also, it's not actually a second-price auction. We're not actually auctioning ad spots to the highest bidder and making them pay the second price. We're actually choosing the ad spots in part based on who the highest bidder is, but in part on relevance. So when you search for toilet paper And we don't want us to show you like sponsored products that are toilet paper. They don't want to show you sponsored products that are like cars, right? Even though that might have a higher margin and might be willing to pay more.
turns.zh: 对。所以如果你的出价高于软保留价，那你就按软保留价成交，因为那是第二高的出价。而如果你的出价低于软保留价，那你就按你自己的价格成交，因为那才是第二高的出价。所以无论哪种情况，你都拿到第二高的出价，只不过这是一场多了一个出价很高的竞价者的拍卖。所以 FTC 认为这一点是决定性的。而我觉得 Amazon 的抗辩非常精彩，因为他们并不说，我们不这么干。他们确实说，我们披露得很清楚。你知道的，他们说，我们其实并没有在这件事上撒谎。我们确实披露了信息。但你知道，FTC 引用了所有这些材料，就是他们发出去那些解释第二价格拍卖的教育性材料给广告主。而 FTC 就说，可那不是你们实际做的。Amazon 就说，看，没有人是基于对拍卖机制的简化描述来买广告的。他们买广告是基于广告支出回报率（return on ad spend），对吧？所以如果你花一块钱、拿回四块钱的收入，你就会说，好啊，太好了，我会继续买广告。Amazon 在这里的抗辩——我觉得是真的——而且它让我觉得很有意思，因为它跟金融行业的运作方式不一样。Amazon 的抗辩基本上是，这就是个黑箱（black box）。我们并不指望我们的广告主真的理解拍卖机制，因为我们做的并不是第二价格拍卖，对吧？就是说，好吧，它是一个带软保留价的第二价格拍卖，但连我们自己都要等到事后才知道软保留价是多少。它是实时计算出来的。所以没人能知道自己会是第二高的价格还是第一高的价格。而且，它其实也不是第二价格拍卖。我们并不是真的把广告位拍卖给出价最高的人、再让他们付第二高的价格。我们实际上选择广告位时，一部分依据是谁出价最高，但另一部分依据是相关性（relevance）。所以当你搜卫生纸的时候，我们不希望给你展示那些是卫生纸的赞助商品。他们不想给你展示那些像汽车这样的赞助商品，对吧？尽管那可能利润率更高、可能愿意出更多的钱。

turns.zh: 我是 Mary Childs。

turns.en: We'll have fill-in guest hosts for a few months while my usual co-host Katie Greifeld is on parental leave. You can find my work by subscribing to the Money Stuff newsletter on Bloomberg.com.
turns.zh: 在我平时的联合主持人 Katie Greifeld 休育儿假（parental leave）的这几个月里，我们会请一些代班的客座主持。你可以在 Bloomberg.com 上订阅 Money Stuff 通讯（newsletter）来找到我的作品。

turns.en: And you can find me at Mary in America on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.
turns.zh: 你可以在 YouTube 上的 Mary in America 找到我，或者在你平时听播客的任何地方。

turns.en: We'd love to hear from you. You can send an email to moneypod at bloomberg.net. Ask us a question and we might answer it on the air. You can also subscribe to our show wherever you're listening right now and leave us a review. It helps more people find the show. The Money Stuff Podcast is produced by Anna Mazarakis and Moses Andon. Our theme music was composed by Blake Maples. Amy Keene is our executive producer and Cheryl Brumley is Bloomberg's head of podcasts. Thanks for listening to the Money Stuff Podcast. We'll be back next week with more stuff.
turns.zh: 我们很想听到你的声音。你可以发邮件到 moneypod@bloomberg.net。给我们提个问题，我们可能会在节目里回答。你也可以在你现在正在收听的平台订阅我们的节目，并给我们留个评价。这能帮更多人发现这档节目。Money Stuff 播客由 Anna Mazarakis 和 Moses Andon 制作。我们的主题音乐由 Blake Maples 作曲。Amy Keene 是我们的执行制作人（executive producer），Cheryl Brumley 是 Bloomberg 的播客主管。感谢收听 Money Stuff 播客。我们下周再见，带来更多 stuff（内容）。
